messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nadia was 69, a married Middle Eastern woman who had spent most of her working life in a fast-food restaurant on the edge of town, where the shift was noisy, bright, and open to the parking lot. Her distress began after a man she barely knew started appearing wherever she went, first outside the shop and then near her apartment building, lingering long enough for her to notice but not long enough for anyone else to take it seriously. He learned her routines, the times she left for work, the route she took home, and the way she looked over her shoulder before getting into her car. One evening, after he had followed her from the restaurant and stood too close by the stairwell, Nadia felt the same cold surge of dread she now associates with that period; from then on she came to believe that people cannot be trusted, and that something in her had changed so much she no longer knew herself. That belief made every unfamiliar face feel loaded with danger. At work she began studying customers and delivery drivers in the same intense way she watched the man who stalked her, reading body language and expression for warning signs, and on the drive home she would circle the block if she saw a car that seemed to be behind her for too long. At night she woke alert, convinced she needed to check whether she was safe, and she repeatedly walked the apartment twice to test doors and windows, a ritual that her husband found exhausting and that gradually made their evenings smaller and more tense.

The more Nadia tried not to think about what happened, the more those thoughts seemed to arrive anyway, carrying images that felt too much to bear. She was certain that if she let herself remember, she would not be able to handle it, so she pushed the memories away, but that effort left the past feeling even more intrusive and harder to contain. When the memory came, it did not come like a story she owned; at times it felt as if it had happened to a stranger, numb and unreal, and at times it was so extreme that she could hardly believe it had happened to her at all. Certain moments brought it back most sharply: the metal stairwell at her building, the sour smell of stale cigarette smoke near the entrance, the faint odor of the grease and onions from the restaurant clinging to her uniform. When those smells surfaced, the scene returned with a force that made her stomach tighten and her mind go blank.

That strange, disconnected quality of remembering fed back into her sense of being changed and unrecognizable. If the event could feel unreal even in her own mind, Nadia would tell herself there must be something wrong with her, that she was not who she had been before and could not trust her own judgment now. From there, mistrust spread outward again: if she could not trust herself to read what was happening, then other people were even less trustworthy. That conclusion kept her scanning faces in the restaurant and bracing whenever a customer paused too long at the counter, and each time she caught herself watching, she felt proof that the world was still dangerous. The danger seemed to justify the vigilance, and the vigilance seemed to confirm the danger. She began sleeping lightly, waking in the night to check locks again, then arriving at work already tense, already studying every stranger who came through the door, already expecting that someone might be waiting outside for her when the shift ended. Over weeks and months she stopped taking the evening walks she once enjoyed with her husband, avoided being alone in the parking lot, and let younger coworkers handle closing whenever she could.

By the time she sought help, Nadia was frightened not only of the man who had stalked her but of the life she had built around being on guard. She was exhausted by checking, scanning, and doubting, yet she remained most afraid that if she relaxed for even a moment, something terrible would happen and she would be blamed for not noticing. What brought her in was how far the fear had spread into sleep, work, and her marriage, and how little of herself she felt she recognized anymore. Above all, she wanted to know whether she could ever feel safe without keeping watch every second.
